option_a: Live a life of complete moral consistency — every value you hold, you act on without exception — but remain unknown and unmourned when you die
option_b: Be celebrated as a moral exemplar by millions, shaping how they treat each other for generations, while privately knowing your life was riddled with hypocrisy
framing: Does moral worth reside in the character of a life as it is lived, or in the effects that life has on the world?

option_a: Retain every memory of your life but slowly lose all sense of who you are — your preferences, your personality, your values dissolve while the record remains intact
option_b: Lose all memory of your life but retain exactly who you are — your character, your values, your way of being in the world unchanged, but the events are gone
framing: Is personal identity constituted by the continuity of psychological states, or by the continuity of the experiential record?

option_a: Know with certainty exactly how and when you will die, but have no ability to change it
option_b: Have complete freedom over how you die but never know when — it could be today, it could be in seventy years
framing: Between certainty that forecloses hope and freedom that forecloses peace, which is the better relationship with your own finitude?

option_a: Discover a scientific truth so powerful and dangerous that sharing it would probably destroy civilization — and publish it anyway, because truth belongs to everyone
option_b: Suppress that same truth forever, carrying it alone, because you believe the consequences of release outweigh any principle about the free flow of knowledge
framing: When knowledge and survival are in conflict, does epistemic duty have limits?

option_a: Be fully understood by every person you meet — your motives, fears, and inner life transparent to them — but lose the ability to understand anyone else
option_b: Have perfect understanding of every person you meet — their full inner world legible to you — but remain completely opaque and unknowable to everyone else
framing: Between being known and knowing others, which form of connection is more constitutive of a full human life?

option_a: Live in a world where every moral question has a single correct, knowable answer — and you always know what it is
option_b: Live in a world where morality is genuinely uncertain and contested, but your choices are entirely your own, shaped by nothing but your own reasoning
framing: Is moral agency more valuable when it operates against a backdrop of objective truth, or when it must constitute that truth itself?

option_a: Spend your entire life building something — an institution, an idea, a movement — that will outlast you by centuries, but never see it finished
option_b: Complete something meaningful within your lifetime that disappears entirely the moment you die, leaving no trace
framing: Does the value of a life's work depend on its continuation beyond the life, or is completion in itself sufficient?

option_a: Have access to perfect information about any factual question you ask, but lose all capacity for intuition, gut feeling, and aesthetic judgment
option_b: Retain full intuition, emotional intelligence, and aesthetic sense, but be unable to know whether any factual belief you hold is actually true
framing: Between propositional knowledge and experiential wisdom, which is the more foundational human faculty?

option_a: Always act freely — every choice you make is genuinely undetermined — but live with complete uncertainty about who you are and what you value
option_b: Have a completely stable, consistent self — your values and character always predictable — but discover your choices are fully determined by causes outside your control
framing: Is freedom from external determination worth more than stability of self, or does genuine selfhood require that very determinism?

option_a: Be the person responsible for a decision that causes great harm to a few but saves many — and carry that knowledge for the rest of your life
option_b: Refuse to make that decision, allowing greater harm to occur, but never bear personal causal responsibility for any death
framing: Is the moral weight of direct causation categorically different from the moral weight of allowing harm through inaction?

option_a: Live in a society of perfect equality — identical resources, opportunities, and outcomes for everyone — but with no mechanism for recognizing or rewarding excellence
option_b: Live in a society that maximizes total human flourishing but requires a permanent underclass whose suffering makes that flourishing possible
framing: Is a just society defined by the equal distribution of goods, or by the aggregate quality of lives lived within it?

option_a: Remember every experience of your life with perfect fidelity — every joy, every humiliation, every grief, in full resolution forever
option_b: Forget most of your life naturally, retaining only the emotional residue of experiences — the shape of things, not the thing itself
framing: Does a full life require the preservation of its moments, or does living forward require the mercy of forgetting?

option_a: Have the power to see the long-term consequences of every significant decision before you make it — including the consequences of your knowledge of the consequences
option_b: Make all decisions in genuine uncertainty, never knowing outcomes in advance, but your choices remain authentically responsive to how things actually unfold
framing: Does foreknowledge of consequences enhance or undermine the moral significance of a choice?

option_a: Be the most powerful person in the world — every decision of consequence flows through you — but be unable to trust that anyone around you is honest with you
option_b: Have no formal power whatsoever, but be surrounded entirely by people who are completely honest with you and whose relationships with you are entirely genuine
framing: Is power without authentic connection a form of isolation — and if so, is that isolation itself a deprivation?

option_a: Experience every emotion at maximum intensity — grief, joy, love, rage, awe — with no dampening, no numbing, and no capacity to regulate
option_b: Live at a stable emotional baseline — never deeply suffering, never deeply elated — with the security of knowing your interior life will never overwhelm you
framing: Is a life of extreme emotional range more fully human than a life of equanimity, even if the former contains far more suffering?

option_a: Exist in a deterministic world — every event causally inevitable from the beginning — but experience your life as if your choices matter
option_b: Exist in a world of genuine randomness — events are not causally determined — but discover this means your choices have no more authorship than a coin flip
framing: If both determinism and indeterminism undermine the intuitive picture of free will, is the concept coherent at all?

option_a: Know that your life has an objective meaning assigned by the nature of the universe itself — and discover that meaning is not what you would have chosen
option_b: Know with certainty that life has no assigned meaning whatsoever — meaning is entirely self-created, radically free, and entirely your responsibility
framing: Between imposed meaning you didn't choose and constructed meaning with no external anchor, which is the firmer basis for a life?

option_a: Be the last person alive — outlive everyone you have ever known or loved by decades — but preserve all records of human civilization for whatever comes after
option_b: Die with everyone you love simultaneously, in the same moment, knowing that human civilization and all its records will be preserved without you
framing: Is the value of surviving others located in the preservation it enables — and if so, what does that say about what survival is for?

option_a: Have the ability to make one irrevocable decision that ends a great injustice immediately but at enormous cost to people who did nothing to cause it
option_b: Work within existing institutions to address the same injustice, knowing it will take generations and many people will suffer unjustly in the meantime
framing: When the pace of justice is itself unjust, does that create a moral obligation to act outside the system?

option_a: Live a long life of moderate but reliable satisfaction — good work, genuine relationships, ordinary joys — with no exceptional highs or lows
option_b: Live a short life of extraordinary intensity — profound love, creative genius, genuine danger — knowing it will end before you are ready
framing: Is the value of a life measured by its duration, its peaks, or something about the integration of both?

option_a: Have your consciousness uploaded and run on hardware indefinitely — all your memories, personality, and reasoning intact — while your biological body ceases
option_b: Continue in your biological body until natural death, knowing that at death everything that is you ends completely and irrevocably
framing: If psychological continuity is preserved but substrate changes entirely, is the uploaded entity the same person — and does the answer change what death means?

option_a: Be the only person in your society who can see the true costs of the things everyone else enjoys — and you are unable to communicate it in a way they will believe
option_b: Share in the general blindness — genuinely unable to perceive those costs — and therefore participate fully in your community without private moral burden
framing: Is it better to perceive an injustice you cannot remedy, or to be constitutionally incapable of perceiving it?

option_a: Live in a world where every person's true beliefs — including their beliefs about you — are fully visible to everyone at all times
option_b: Live in the current world, where privacy of thought is absolute — people can deceive, withhold, and perform, and you can never know what they truly think
framing: Does radical transparency enable authentic community, or destroy the conditions under which authentic relationships are possible?

option_a: Create a work of art that will be considered the greatest human achievement of its kind for a thousand years, but produce nothing else of value in your entire life
option_b: Produce a steady body of honest, skilled, genuinely useful work across your entire life — work that matters to the people who encounter it — but nothing that will be remembered
framing: Is the value of creative work located in its singular excellence or in its continuous presence in lives?

option_a: Always know when you are being irrational — your biases and motivated reasoning visible to you in real time — but knowing does not make you more rational
option_b: Be constitutionally immune to self-awareness of your own irrationality — your reasoning always feels sound to you — but your actual reasoning is no worse than average
framing: Is the discomfort of self-knowledge about cognitive limitation worth more than the peace of its absence?

option_a: Live in a just society that you did nothing to build — its fairness a gift you inherited — and you are unable to improve it further
option_b: Live in an unjust society and spend your life working to make it marginally more just — knowing you will not see the full results of your effort
framing: Is moral meaning derived more from inhabiting good conditions or from striving to create them?

option_a: Have your deepest held convictions tested against perfect counterarguments — and discover that after honest engagement, you cannot rationally defend any of them
option_b: Never encounter a serious challenge to your convictions — they remain intact and motivating — but you suspect, with no way to resolve it, that they might not survive scrutiny
framing: Between beliefs that cannot survive examination and beliefs never subjected to it, which provides the better basis for a life?

option_a: Be the person who discovers that a beloved institution was founded on a deliberate lie, and must decide whether to reveal it
option_b: Live inside that same institution, never knowing the truth, benefiting from the stability and meaning it provides, the lie invisible to you
framing: When a lie is the foundation of something genuinely good, does revealing it serve truth or destroy value?

option_a: Have the ability to feel exactly what another person feels — their physical sensations, emotions, and private experience — whenever you choose to invoke it
option_b: Lose all ability to infer or imagine what others feel, becoming constitutionally unable to empathize, but gain complete clarity about your own inner states
framing: Between radical empathy that risks dissolving the self and radical self-clarity that forecloses other-understanding, which is the better basis for moral life?

option_a: Be given, at birth, a complete and accurate account of the historical injustices that produced your current advantages — and feel their full moral weight for the rest of your life
option_b: Remain in ordinary ignorance of those same injustices — benefiting from them without awareness, and therefore without the specific burden of knowing
framing: Does moral responsibility require awareness of its grounds, or does it bind regardless of what we know?

option_a: Live in a world where human consciousness can be perfectly transferred between bodies — aging, disease, and death become optional — but identity becomes uncertain and contested
option_b: Live in the current world, where consciousness is inseparable from the body it inhabits — death is real and final — but what you are is never in question
framing: Is the certainty of identity worth the certainty of death?

option_a: Always act on the rule that would be best if everyone followed it — even in cases where breaking it would produce obviously better consequences in that specific moment
option_b: Always act to produce the best consequences in each specific situation — even when doing so requires breaking rules that are generally beneficial and that others depend on
framing: Does morality require fidelity to principles that transcend outcomes, or is it ultimately about making the world go better?

option_a: Possess complete certainty about every ethical question — you always know the right thing to do — but others perceive your certainty as arrogance and refuse to follow
option_b: Possess genuine moral uncertainty about most questions — your reasoning humble and revisable — but your openness is so persuasive that others consistently defer to your judgment
framing: Between rightness that cannot persuade and persuasion that may not be right, which is the better moral position?

option_a: Know that in two hundred years your name will be attached to a great harm — not because you intended it, but because your work was used in ways you could not foresee
option_b: Know that in two hundred years your name will be entirely forgotten — your work made the world slightly better, but left no trace that can be attributed to you
framing: Between legacy that is remembered wrongly and goodness that is not remembered at all, which is the better way to matter?

option_a: Have perfect recall of every conversation you have ever had — every word, every tone, every detail — and never be able to let any of them go
option_b: Remember only the emotional truth of your relationships — the feeling of a person, not the record of interactions — and discover that some people you love are becoming strangers
framing: Is the substance of a relationship located in its events or in its felt quality — and can you have both?

option_a: Be the architect of a world in which suffering is abolished — no pain, no grief, no loss — but in which the depth of joy, beauty, and love is correspondingly diminished
option_b: Live in the current world, in which suffering is real and sometimes devastating, but joy, beauty, and love can reach intensities unavailable to a being that cannot suffer
framing: Is the capacity for suffering constitutive of the capacity for flourishing, or merely contingently correlated with it?

option_a: Have the power to know, for any person you meet, whether they are acting out of genuine virtue or out of self-interest disguised as virtue
option_b: Live in the current world, unable to make that distinction, and therefore required to extend trust without certainty
framing: Would the ability to detect moral inauthenticity improve human life, or destroy the conditions under which genuine trust is possible?

option_a: Be the last generation — your children will not exist — in exchange for the guarantee that every person alive today lives out their full potential
option_b: Allow the continuation of human generations indefinitely, with all the ordinary mixture of flourishing and suffering that implies, knowing your own life is unremarkable within it
framing: Does the moral value of future people create obligations that can outweigh present ones?

option_a: Live in a world where your choices are genuinely free, but the chain of consequences from each choice is totally opaque to you
option_b: Live in a world where every consequence of your choices is perfectly visible before you act, but you discover this visibility makes real choice feel impossible
framing: Is the experience of freedom compatible with full knowledge of what that freedom produces?

option_a: Have your consciousness persist after death as an observer — fully aware, unable to interact, watching the world continue without you indefinitely
option_b: Have your consciousness end completely at death — no experience of any kind — but know with certainty before you die that this is what happens
framing: Between disembodied persistence without participation and complete cessation with foreknowledge, which is the less bad form of ending?

option_a: Be the person who must decide, with incomplete information and under time pressure, which of two communities receives a scarce resource that will save most of them
option_b: Be a member of one of those communities, with no decision-making power, whose survival depends entirely on how that person decides
framing: Is the moral burden of power over life and death better located in the person who holds it or the person subject to it?

option_a: Live with the ability to perceive beauty everywhere — in mathematics, in strangers, in decay, in the ordinary — but be unable to communicate what you perceive to anyone
option_b: Lose the capacity for aesthetic experience entirely, but gain the ability to communicate with perfect clarity and precision everything you think and feel
framing: Between a rich private world and a fully shared one, which is the more complete form of human life?

option_a: Know with certainty that consciousness is entirely physical — there is nothing it is like to be you beyond the firing of neurons — and live with that knowledge
option_b: Know with certainty that consciousness is irreducibly non-physical — there is something it is like to be you that escapes physical explanation — but be unable to prove it to anyone
framing: Does the truth about the nature of consciousness change the value or meaning of the experience of being conscious?

option_a: Be given complete information about every way in which your personality and values were shaped by forces outside your control — genetics, trauma, culture, chance
option_b: Remain in ordinary ignorance of those influences, experiencing your values and personality as genuinely your own even if they are not
framing: Does self-knowledge about the origins of the self undermine or deepen the sense of ownership over it?

option_a: Have the power to redistribute wealth such that no one on earth suffers from material deprivation — at the cost of a permanent reduction in total innovation and discovery
option_b: Preserve the current system of incentives for innovation and discovery, knowing it will produce extraordinary advances but maintain significant material suffering for many
framing: When eliminating suffering requires accepting permanent limits on human potential, is that trade morally required?

option_a: Live in a world where every human has exactly the same moral status and no special obligations to family, friends, or community over strangers
option_b: Live in the current world, where we are permitted — perhaps required — to favor those close to us, even when doing so comes at real cost to strangers
framing: Is moral impartiality an ideal to be approximated or a distortion of what morality actually requires?

option_a: Have access to every piece of knowledge humanity has produced — every scientific paper, every work of literature, every historical record — but lose the ability to generate new ideas
option_b: Lose access to all accumulated human knowledge, retaining only what you currently hold in memory, but gain an extraordinary capacity for original thought
framing: Is knowledge more valuable as inheritance or as creation?

option_a: Be a person whose character is fixed at birth — your virtues and vices determined, your arc of growth complete before it begins
option_b: Be a person whose character is entirely plastic — capable of becoming anyone, in any direction, throughout your life — with no stable core
framing: Is the value of character located in its stability or in its capacity for transformation?

option_a: Know for certain that the universe is indifferent to human existence — no design, no purpose, no witness — but that human value is therefore entirely self-generated
option_b: Know for certain that the universe is structured around something like purpose — but that purpose is entirely opaque to human understanding
framing: Between a universe of self-made meaning and a universe of hidden meaning, which provides the better grounds for living?

option_a: Have the ability to forgive completely — releasing all resentment, genuinely wishing well to those who harmed you — but only by losing the memory of the harm
option_b: Retain perfect memory of every harm done to you, unable to fully forgive, but also unable to let the harm define you more than it already has
framing: Is genuine forgiveness possible without forgetting — and if it requires forgetting, is it still forgiveness?
